entries.narration: Start with one order in a small online shop. A shopper clicks Place order, and three quite different kinds of message start moving around. The first is a command. Place order is a request, and a request can be refused: the card might be declined, or an item might be out of stock. The second is an event. Once the checkout service has accepted the order, it records a fact: order placed. An event is in the past tense, because it describes something that has already happened and cannot be refused any more. The third is state. Order ten forty-two is currently placed, and later it will be shipped. State is a summary of everything that has happened so far, and it keeps changing. Kafka is built around the second kind, the event. The checkout service publishes the fact once, and then it is done. Fulfilment, analytics and notifications each react to that fact on their own schedule, and none of them needs checkout to wait for it. That independence is the reason to communicate asynchronously, and it is what the rest of this course builds on.

Here is the same order handled two ways. In the top picture, checkout calls each interested service directly, one after another. That looks simple, but it quietly makes every one of those services part of placing an order. If fulfilment is down, checkout fails, even though nothing was wrong with the order. If analytics is slow, every shopper waits for analytics. And when the business wants receipts emailed, someone has to change checkout and redeploy it. In the bottom picture, checkout appends one event to a log and immediately returns to the shopper. The log keeps that event. Fulfilment reads it when it is ready, analytics catches up later, and a notifications service added next month can still read orders that arrived before it existed. Nobody waits for anybody. That is what asynchronous means here: the writer and the readers no longer have to be available, or fast, at the same moment. The price is that results are no longer immediate, and the rest of this course is largely about managing that price carefully.

Before looking inside Kafka, it helps to place it among the older ways of moving data between systems. With request and response, one caller asks and waits for one answer, and once the answer arrives there is nothing left to read again. A work queue spreads messages across many workers, but each message goes to exactly one of them and is removed once it has been handled. That is ideal for sharing out work, and wrong when two different teams both need every order. A batch file, say a nightly export, does contain everything, but it only arrives on a schedule, and tomorrow's file replaces today's. A retained log is the fourth style, and it is the one Kafka implements. Records are appended in order and kept for a configured period, whether or not anyone has read them. Any number of independent readers can read the whole log, each at its own pace, and any of them can go back and read it again. Keep the three questions at the bottom in mind: who reads, when, and can they read it again. They are the quickest way to decide whether a log is actually the right tool.

This is the single idea that most separates Kafka from a message queue. In a queue, reading a message takes it away. In a Kafka log, reading takes nothing away. Each reader simply keeps a position, a number that says which record it will read next. Here, fulfilment has handled everything up to offset three, so its next offset is four. Analytics is far behind, and its next offset is one. Both of them are looking at exactly the same records, and neither position has any effect on the log or on the other reader. Analytics can be slow for an hour, and fulfilment never notices. So what does remove records? Retention. The topic is configured to keep records for a period of time, or up to a size, and once records fall outside that limit they are deleted, whether or not anyone ever read them. That has a consequence worth remembering already: a reader that falls further behind than the retention period does not just lag. It loses data, because the records it still needed are gone.

A record is the unit that Kafka stores and delivers, so it is worth knowing exactly what is in one. The producer supplies four things. The key, here the order identifier, is what decides which partition the record goes to, and that turns out to matter a great deal for ordering. The value is the event itself, often JSON, or a typed schema format, which comes up in the next chapter. Headers are optional key and value pairs for metadata, such as where the order came from. And the timestamp, which by default the producer sets to the time it created the record. Notice that Kafka does not interpret the key or the value. To the broker they are just bytes, and the meaning belongs entirely to the applications on either side. The second table is where the record ends up. The producer names the topic. The partition is chosen from the key. And the offset, the record's position in that partition, is assigned by the broker at the moment it appends the record. The producer never picks an offset, and once assigned, it never changes.

A topic is a named stream of records, orders in this case, but it is not stored as one long log. It is split into partitions, three here, and each partition is its own ordered log with its own offsets, each counting up from zero. When checkout sends a record with a key, the default partitioner hashes the key and takes the result modulo the number of partitions. These are the real results for these keys: o-ten forty lands in partition zero, ten forty-one in partition one, and ten forty-two in partition two. Because the same key always hashes to the same partition, every event about order ten forty-one lands in partition one, in the order it was written, so placed always comes before paid. That is the ordering guarantee Kafka gives, and it is per partition. Now look at what offsets do not tell you. Offset one in partition zero and offset one in partition one are unrelated records. There is no single order across the whole topic, and if your design needs one, that need has to be dealt with in how you choose keys and topics, which is exactly where the next chapter starts.

There are four roles to know, and only one of them stores anything. A producer is any application that writes records, checkout in our example. Brokers are the Kafka servers. They store the partitions on disk and handle every read and write, and in a real cluster the partitions of one topic are spread across several brokers. A consumer is an application instance that reads records. The fourth role is the one people most often misunderstand: the consumer group. A group is the set of consumers that together make up one application, sharing its work. Inside a group, each partition is read by exactly one member at a time, so fulfilment's two members split the three partitions between them. But groups do not share with each other. Analytics is a separate group, so it reads every record too, with its own positions, at its own speed. That is how one stream of orders can feed many applications at once: one group per application, and as many members inside a group as there are partitions to share.

To make this concrete, here is a working cluster on one machine, following the official Kafka four point one quick start. The first command gives the new cluster an identifier, and format writes that identifier into the storage directory, which Kafka refuses to start without. The next command starts the server. In this configuration a single process plays two roles. It is a broker, storing data and serving clients, and it is a controller, managing the cluster's metadata. That is KRaft mode, and it is the only mode Kafka four supports. Older material will mention ZooKeeper, which used to do the controller's job and has now been removed. Then the topic. The quick start creates its topic with whatever the defaults are, and the shipped configuration defaults to a single partition. So this version names three partitions explicitly, because a one-partition topic would hide everything interesting about keys. Finally, describe shows what was actually created. You do not need to run any of this to follow the course. The transcripts that follow show what it produces.

Now the first real trace. In the first terminal, the console producer turns each line you type into a record, and because parse key is set, the text before the colon becomes the key. Three orders go in: ten forty-one, then ten forty-two, then ten forty. In the second terminal, the console consumer reads from the beginning and prints the partition, the offset and the key in front of each value. Every order landed in the partition its key hashes to, and each one is at offset zero, because each is the first record in its partition. Look at the order of the output, though. Ten forty comes out first, even though it was sent last. The consumer reads partitions independently, so the output follows partitions, not the order of sending, and across partitions it can differ from one run to the next. That is the per-partition ordering rule from earlier, seen in a real transcript. And notice what the consumer did not do. It removed nothing. Run the same command again and it prints the same three orders.

The previous consumer had no group name, so it got a random throwaway group and remembered nothing. This time each terminal names a group: fulfilment and analytics. A group's progress is stored in Kafka itself, as committed offsets, and that gives the consumer a memory. In step one, both groups start and both print all three orders, because they are independent. In step two, fulfilment is stopped, and as it shuts down it commits how far it got. In step three a new order arrives. O-ten forty-three hashes to partition one, where it becomes offset one. Analytics is running, so it prints it straight away. In step four, fulfilment is started again, with exactly the same command. It does not print all four orders. It resumes from its committed offsets and prints only the one it missed. The reason is that from beginning is only a fallback: it applies when the group has no committed offsets at all. Once a group has committed, its committed position wins. That is a disconnected reader catching up, and it is the behaviour that makes a log safe to depend on.

Before moving on, be clear about what this little cluster is and is not. It is one process, holding one copy of every partition. That is plenty to see records, keys, partitions, consumer groups and replay working, which is everything in this chapter. What it cannot show is the part that makes Kafka dependable. With one broker, losing that broker means losing the data, and there is nothing to fail over to, no replication, no leader election, and no moving partitions between machines. All of that needs several brokers, and it is chapter five's subject. Three habits are worth forming now. Keep it on localhost, because this configuration is plaintext with no authentication at all. Create topics explicitly, because automatic topic creation is switched on by default, and a mistyped topic name in a producer will silently create a brand new topic with default settings. And when you want a clean slate, stop everything and delete the data directories, knowing that this deletes every topic. Next, the course turns to designing events and topics around their business meaning.

The first design decision for any event stream is where one topic ends and the next begins, and it is mostly a decision about ordering. Kafka keeps records in order only within a single partition of a single topic. Two topics are two unrelated logs. So look at the left-hand design, which feels tidy: one topic for placed orders, one for paid, one for shipped. A reader subscribed to all three can easily see the payment for an order before it sees the order itself, because nothing relates the position in one topic to the position in another. Every reader then has to buffer and reassemble the lifecycle on its own. The right-hand design puts every event about an order into one topic, keyed by the order id, with a field saying which kind of event each record is. Now one order's events always sit in one partition, in the order they were written. The price is that a reader interested only in shipments has to read past the other types and skip them. A useful rule of thumb: events that must be read in order relative to each other belong in the same topic, with the same key.

As soon as a second team reads a topic, that topic has become an interface, just as binding as an API. It needs an owner. Here, the checkout team is the only writer of the orders topic, and it is the team that answers when something about it goes wrong, and that approves any change. Look at what readers are quietly depending on. Fulfilment depends on the key, because the key is what keeps one order's events in order. Analytics depends on the schema to understand every field. Anyone who needs to replay depends on the retention period being long enough. Change any of these, and you have changed something for every reader, whether or not they were told. The name matters too. A good name says what is inside, a domain and an entity, such as shop dot orders, rather than which team or application happens to write it today, because teams and applications get renamed and replaced. Keep the name stable, and if the meaning of the data changes, publish a new topic rather than quietly repurposing the old one. In the rest of this course the examples keep the short name orders, for readability.

Choosing the key is choosing two things at once: which records stay in order relative to each other, and how evenly the work spreads across partitions. Take the four candidates for the orders topic. The order id keeps every event about one order in sequence, and because there are thousands of orders, it spreads the load evenly. That is why it is the default choice for this example. The customer id keeps all of a customer's orders together, which is useful if readers need a customer's history in order. But if a handful of business customers place most of the orders, their partitions carry far more than their share. Region is the trap. It looks like a sensible grouping, but there are only three values, so at most three partitions ever receive anything, however many the topic has. And with no key at all, records are spread evenly, but nothing at all is kept in order. The practical rule is to key by the entity whose events must stay ordered, and then to check that the key has many values with roughly similar traffic. The next section shows what happens when it does not.

Here is the region key in practice, and the partition numbers are real. With three partitions, the default partitioner's hash sends both eu and us to partition one, apac to partition two, and nothing at all to partition zero. Now assume, for this example, that eu and us together are eighty percent of the orders. Partition one carries most of the traffic. In the fulfilment group, the member that owns partition one falls further and further behind, while one member has nothing to do and the third is mostly idle. Lag is growing, but only on one partition. The tempting fix is to add more members to the group, and it does nothing, because a partition is read by only one member of a group at a time. The extra member just waits. Adding partitions does not rescue it either: three key values can still reach, at most, three partitions, and they might collide again. The real fix is a different key, and that is much easier to choose before the topic has years of history and readers depending on the current one. Chapter ten comes back to diagnosing hot partitions from metrics.

Offsets tell you the order in which the broker received records, and it is easy to assume that is the order in which things happened. It is not always. Look at partition one of the orders topic. The first three records are in time order: order ten forty-one placed, ten forty-three placed, and ten forty-one paid. Then comes offset three, order ten fifty, placed at twelve minutes fifty-eight seconds past nine, more than a minute before any of the records above it. It was placed from a phone that had lost its connection, and the app only sent it once it was back online. So there are three different clocks to keep apart. Event time is when the thing actually happened, and it should travel inside the event. Offset order is when the broker appended it. Processing time is when a reader gets round to handling it, which might be seconds or hours later. Ordering by offset is still correct for one order's lifecycle. But anything that groups by time, such as sales per minute, has to use event time and has to decide how long to wait for late records. Kafka Streams handles exactly this in chapter eight.

Partition counts are often picked casually and then increased when traffic grows. Kafka allows that, but only upwards: a topic's partition count can be increased and never decreased. The catch is in the partitioner. It computes the hash of the key, modulo the number of partitions, so changing the number of partitions changes the answer. These are the real placements for five orders. Going from three partitions to four, four of the five keys hash somewhere new. Only order ten forty-three stays put. Nothing already written moves. Existing records stay exactly where they are, and only new records follow the new placement. So consider order ten forty-one. Its placed and paid events are in partition one. Its shipped event, written after the change, lands in partition zero. A reader can now see shipped before paid, because the two events are in different partitions. That breaks per-key ordering across the change. It may be brief, but it is real. So choose a partition count up front with room to grow, and where ordering really matters, stop the writers during the change, or migrate to a new topic instead.

Between the producer and the consumer, Kafka never sees an order. It sees bytes. In the producer application, a serializer turns the order object into bytes. The broker stores those bytes and hands them out again unchanged. In the consumer, a deserializer turns them back into an object, and that only works if it understands the format the serializer used. The important consequence is that the broker does not check anything. A record with malformed JSON, or the wrong fields, or even the wrong format entirely, is stored and replicated just like a good one. Nobody finds out until a reader tries to deserialize it and fails, possibly hours later, in a different team's application. So the writer and the reader have to agree on a format, and that agreement lives outside Kafka. JSON is the common starting point. It is readable and every language handles it, but nothing enforces its shape. Avro and Protobuf are compact binary formats with a schema that defines every field and its type. That schema is what makes the contract checkable, which is what the next sections are about.

Schemas change, and the producers and consumers of a busy topic cannot all be upgraded at the same moment. Compatibility is the rule that says which versions can still read each other's data during that transition. There are two directions, and the names are easy to mix up, so phrase them as who reads whom. Backward compatibility means new readers can read old data. If you have that, upgrade the consumers first, because the data they meet will still be old for a while. Forward compatibility means old readers can read new data. Then the producers can upgrade first, because consumers that have not been upgraded will still cope. Full compatibility gives both, so either side can go first. And none means nothing is checked, and everyone must change at once. The code card shows how a single default makes a change safe. Version two adds a channel field with a default of web. An old reader simply ignores the new field. A new reader reading an old record fills in web. That one default keeps the change compatible in both directions.

Here are five common schema changes, each checked in both directions, under Avro's rules. Protobuf and JSON Schema have their own rules, so treat this table as Avro-specific. Every row follows from just two rules, both applied to the reader's schema. First, if the data contains a field the reader does not know, the reader skips it. Second, if the reader expects a field the data does not contain, it needs a default for that field in its own schema, or the read fails. Now the rows. Adding a field with a default: old readers skip it, and new readers use the default for old records. Safe both ways. Adding a field with no default: old readers are still fine, but a new reader meeting an old record has nothing to fill the field with, and fails. Removing a field that had a default is safe, and removing one without a default breaks old readers of new data. A rename is the nasty one. To Avro it is a removal plus an addition, so it fails both ways, unless the new reader declares the old name as an alias. A registry can run exactly these checks before a new version is accepted.

A schema registry is the usual way to make the contract enforceable. It stores every version of every schema, and it checks each new version against the compatibility rule before accepting it. It is worth being precise about what it is. It is a separate service in the Kafka ecosystem, such as Confluent Schema Registry or Apicurio. It is not part of Apache Kafka, and the broker knows nothing about it. Here is how a record finds its schema. The producer uses a registry-aware serializer. The first time it sends order placed version two, the serializer registers the schema and gets back an id, seven in this example. From then on, each record carries just a small header with that id, followed by the encoded order, rather than the whole schema. In Confluent's wire format that is one magic byte and four bytes of id. The consumer's deserializer reads the id, fetches schema seven once, and caches it. Notice what the registry does not do. The broker still stores opaque bytes and checks nothing. A producer that skips the registry-aware serializer can still write anything at all.

A schema fixes the shape of an event. A good contract goes further and fixes what the fields mean, and what must never appear in them. Three fields earn a place in almost every event. An event id, unique to this one event, so that a reader who receives the same event twice can recognise the duplicate. Chapter three shows why duplicates happen even when nothing is wrong. An occurred at timestamp, the event time, set by the writer when the thing happened, for the reasons from the section on time. And the entity id that is also the key, here the order id. Just as important is what stays out. This event refers to the customer by id. It does not carry their name, address or card number. Retention keeps every copy of every record for days or longer, often replicated to other systems, and you cannot reach into a log and edit a single record later. Sensitive data put into an event is very hard to take back. Finally, validate events before producing them, against the schema and against these rules, because the broker will accept whatever it is given.

Publishing from Java starts with one object, the Kafka producer. It is designed to be long-lived and thread-safe, so the normal pattern is one producer per application, shared by every thread that publishes, and closed once, when the application shuts down. Creating it needs very little. Bootstrap servers is a list of brokers to make first contact with. It does not need to name every broker, because the producer discovers the rest. Then two serializers, one for the key and one for the value, which turn them into bytes. Everything else has a default, and in Kafka four point one those defaults favour safety over speed, which is the right starting point. Behind that small amount of code, the producer owns real resources: a background sender thread, network connections to the brokers it uses, and a memory buffer for records that have not been sent yet. That is why creating a new producer for every send is such a common performance bug. And it is why closing matters. Close waits for pending sends to finish, then releases everything. The try with resources block here does exactly that.

A producer does not send everything to one broker and let it forward records around the cluster. Every partition has one broker acting as its leader, and the producer sends each batch directly to that leader. So before it can send anything, the producer has to find out who leads what. It connects to one of the bootstrap brokers and asks for the topic's metadata. The answer lists every partition, the broker currently leading it, and the address to reach that broker. Here, partition zero is led by broker one, partition one by broker two, and partition two by broker three. The producer caches that map and refreshes it periodically. Leadership does change, for example while a broker is restarted for maintenance. When that happens, a batch can arrive at a broker that is no longer the leader. That broker replies with a not leader error, which is retriable. The producer refreshes its metadata, learns the new leader, and sends the batch again, and the application never sees any of it. One practical consequence: every client must be able to reach every broker's advertised address, which matters a great deal in chapter nine.

The most important thing to understand about send is what it does not do. It does not wait for a broker. It serializes the record, places it in the producer's buffer, and returns, usually within microseconds. At that point nothing has been stored anywhere. The record is just waiting in memory. The outcome arrives later, in one of two ways. The callback you pass to send runs exactly once, with the record's topic, partition and offset if it was stored, or with an exception if it was not. Send also returns a future, which gives the same answer if you block on it. Blocking on every send, one at a time, is tempting because it feels safe, but it throws away batching and can cut throughput dramatically. Callbacks have one important rule. They run on the producer's own I O thread, the same thread that sends every batch. Anything slow in a callback, like a database call, holds up every other send from this producer. So keep callbacks short. Note the outcome, and when something failed, record it somewhere durable so it can be dealt with deliberately rather than lost.

A failed publish does not always look like an exception at the call site. It can appear in three different places, and an application has to handle all three. First, send itself throws, but only for problems on the application's side, such as a value the serializer cannot handle. Second, and most commonly, the callback receives the error. That is where anything reported by a broker or the network ends up. Third, flush and close. Both block until pending records have finished, one way or the other, so a shutdown that does not wait for them can silently drop whatever was still in the buffer. The errors themselves come in two kinds. Retriable errors, like a leader that has just moved, or a temporary timeout, are retried by the producer on its own, and the application only hears about them if retries run out. Non-retriable errors, like a record larger than the broker accepts, or a failed authentication, are reported straight away, because retrying cannot help. One error deserves special care: a delivery timeout. It means the producer gave up waiting. It does not mean the record was not stored.

Underneath send, the producer is not sending records one at a time. For every partition it keeps one open batch, and each new record for that partition is appended to it. A batch is sent as a single request in one of two situations: when it reaches batch size, sixteen kilobytes by default, or when it has waited for linger milliseconds, which is five milliseconds by default since Kafka four point oh. Whichever happens first wins. So on this screen, partition one's batch is full and goes immediately, partition two's small batch has waited five milliseconds and goes too, and partition zero's batch is still filling. Even a very quiet partition sends within a few milliseconds. All of these open batches live inside a fixed memory buffer, thirty-two mebibytes by default. Normally it never comes close to full. But if the brokers slow down, or become unreachable, batches cannot leave, and the buffer fills. Then send stops returning immediately. It blocks, for up to max block milliseconds, sixty seconds by default, and then fails. That is the moment a slow cluster becomes a slow application.

Once batching is clear, the throughput settings follow naturally. Larger batches mean fewer requests for the same data, better compression, and more throughput from the same brokers. The cost is a little latency, and some memory. Linger milliseconds is the main lever. Waiting a little longer gives each batch time to fill, which matters most at moderate traffic. Batch size sets how large a batch for one partition may grow. Compression type compresses whole batches. The broker stores them compressed and consumers decompress them, so compression saves network and disk on every hop, at the cost of CPU in the producer and consumers. L Z four and snappy are fast with a moderate ratio. Z standard and gzip squeeze harder for more CPU. Two cautions. None of these settings changes what a successful send means. That is the acks setting, which comes next. And compression works on batches, so when batches are tiny, because linger is zero or traffic is very light, it achieves very little. As always with tuning, measure under realistic traffic before changing anything. Chapter ten covers how.

The acks setting answers a simple question: when does the broker tell the producer that a send succeeded? And because the callback reports success at that moment, it decides what success actually guarantees. With acks zero, the producer does not wait for any answer at all. It is the fastest, and it means a failure on the broker's side is never even reported. With acks one, the leader replies as soon as it has written the record to its own log. That sounds safe, but if the leader fails before its followers have copied the record, a follower becomes leader without it, and the record is gone, even though the producer was told it succeeded. With acks all, which has been the default since Kafka three point oh, the leader waits until every in-sync replica has the record, and only then replies. The picture shows that flow for three replicas. There is one subtlety to carry forward. The in-sync set is not fixed. If followers fall behind, it can shrink, in the worst case to the leader alone, and then acks all quietly means acks one. The setting that prevents that is min in-sync replicas, and chapter five puts the two together.

Some failures leave the producer genuinely unable to know what happened, and the lost acknowledgement is the classic one. This timeline has idempotence switched off, to show the underlying problem. The producer sends order ten forty-one paid. The broker appends it at offset seven, and replies. But the reply is lost on the network. From the producer's side, nothing comes back. After the request timeout, thirty seconds by default, it has to decide what to do, and it cannot tell this situation apart from one where the batch never reached the broker at all. Both look exactly the same: silence. Retries are on, so it sends the same batch again. The broker has no way to recognise it, and appends a second copy at offset eight. This time the reply arrives, and the callback reports a single success. The application believes it published once. The log contains the event twice. There are two lessons here. A timeout is an unknown outcome, not a failure. And retrying turns maybe lost into maybe duplicated. The next sections show how Kafka removes this particular duplicate, and which duplicates it cannot remove.

Retries can change the order of records as well as their number. To keep throughput up, a producer sends a new request to a partition's leader before the previous one has been answered, up to five requests in flight by default. Here, batch A carries order ten forty-one placed, and batch B, sent right behind it, carries ten forty-one paid. Batch A fails, because the leader has just moved. Batch B arrives a moment later, at the new leader, and succeeds, at offset two. Then batch A is retried, and succeeds, at offset three. Both records are in the log, each exactly once, but the order is wrong. Any reader now sees the order paid before it was placed, which is precisely the per-key ordering the key was chosen to protect. There are two ways to prevent this. With idempotence on, which is the default, each batch carries a sequence number. The broker refuses to accept batch B before batch A, so order is kept with up to five requests in flight. Without idempotence, the only protection is allowing a single request in flight at a time, which costs a great deal of throughput.

Idempotence is Kafka's answer to both problems you have just seen. When it is on, the broker assigns each producer a producer id, and the producer numbers its batches for each partition: twelve, thirteen, and so on. Now replay the lost acknowledgement. The retry arrives carrying sequence twelve again. The broker has already appended twelve, so it recognises the retry, writes nothing, and simply replies with success. One send, one record. The same sequence numbers stop reordering, because the broker will not accept thirteen before twelve. It is switched on by default in Kafka four point one, but it has conditions: acks must be all, retries must be enabled, and there may be at most five requests in flight. Here is the trap. If you set acks to one, and do not explicitly ask for idempotence, the producer quietly switches idempotence off, with only an informational log line. If you do explicitly enable it, the same setting is a configuration error instead. Finally, the boundary. Idempotence only covers retries inside one producer instance. A restarted application gets a new producer id, and a deliberate re-send gets a new sequence number.

Idempotence removes duplicates caused by the producer's own retries. It cannot help with a duplicate the application creates itself. Here is the common way that happens. Checkout publishes order ten forty-one paid, and the callback reports a delivery timeout. Remember, that means unknown, not failed. In fact, the record was stored at offset seven. Checkout, believing it failed, publishes the event again, through a new send with a new sequence number, and it is stored again at offset nine. Kafka did nothing wrong. It received two separate sends. The only thing that reveals the truth is that both records carry the same event id, because checkout re-sent the same event rather than building a new one. So this is the publishing policy worth adopting. Validate before sending, because a record that fails validation will fail every time, and retrying it only delays the alert. On a re-send, always reuse the event id. Bound retries by time, and when they run out, park the event somewhere durable and alert a person, rather than retrying forever. And design readers to deduplicate by event id, which is where chapter six picks up.

Consuming in Java looks like producing at first, with a few properties and a client object, but the shape of the code is different. A Kafka consumer does nothing by itself. The application drives it from a loop. Configure a group id, which names the application, and two deserializers, which turn bytes back into keys and values. Subscribe to the topic. Then loop: each call to poll fetches a batch of records, up to five hundred by default, from the partitions this member owns. Process them, in order, and poll again. When the application stops, close leaves the group cleanly, so its partitions can be handed to another member straight away rather than after a timeout. Three rules follow from this design. Unlike the producer, a consumer is not thread-safe, so exactly one thread drives each consumer. The loop's pace matters: a member that stops calling poll for five minutes is treated as failed, and loses its partitions. And deserialization happens inside poll, so a record that cannot be deserialized makes poll itself fail. Chapter six deals with such poison records.

Four numbers describe how far a group has got through one partition, and mixing them up causes most consumer bugs. Here, offsets five and six are done, seven is being processed, and eight has not been fetched. The position is the next offset this member will fetch: eight. It lives only in the consumer's memory, and it moves forward every time poll returns records. The committed offset is the next offset the group should read after a restart: seven. It is stored in Kafka, in an internal topic, and it only moves when the application commits. The log end offset is where the next record will be appended: nine. And lag, the number monitoring dashboards show, is the log end offset minus the committed offset: two. The detail that trips people up is what a committed offset means. Committing seven does not mean seven is done. It means everything before seven is done, and seven is next. Notice also that the position always runs ahead of the commit while a batch is being processed, and only the committed offset survives a crash or a rebalance. That gap is exactly where the next section's failure windows live.

A consumer can crash at any moment, and what that costs depends on where the crash lands relative to the commit. Take a batch of offsets seven to nine. If the consumer processes the batch and then commits ten, a crash after processing but before the commit means the restarted member reads from the old commit, seven, and processes the whole batch again. Nothing is lost, but work is repeated. A crash after the commit costs nothing at all. Now reverse the order. If the consumer commits ten first and then processes, a crash between the two means the restarted member starts at ten. Offsets seven to nine were never processed, and nothing will ever process them. That is data loss. So where does auto-commit fit? It runs inside poll, every five seconds, and it commits the offsets of the records the previous poll returned. If all processing happens inside the loop, before the next poll, that is effectively process then commit, so it replays and never loses. But if the loop hands records to other threads and polls straight away, auto-commit can commit records those threads have not finished.

To control the crash window, most applications switch auto-commit off and commit explicitly, at the one point where it is safe. Set enable auto commit to false. Process every record returned by the poll, completely, including any database writes. Then call commit sync. With no arguments, it commits the positions the consumer has just reached, which means everything returned by that poll. Commit sync waits for the broker to confirm, retries what can be retried, and throws if the commit fails, so a failure is visible to the code. Commit async does not wait. It is faster, and if one asynchronous commit fails, the next successful one covers it, which is why it is common to commit asynchronously in the loop and synchronously once on shutdown. Whichever you use, commit per batch rather than per record, because every commit is itself a write to Kafka. And be clear about the guarantee you have bought. Committing after processing means a crash can still repeat a batch, so this is at least once. Making that repetition harmless is chapter six's subject.

Inside a group, Kafka assigns every partition to exactly one member. That single rule decides how far a group can scale. The orders topic has three partitions, so the fulfilment group can keep at most three members busy. Here it has four. Members one, two and three each own one partition, and member four gets nothing at all. It is not broken. It is an idle standby, which will take over a partition if another member leaves, but until then it does no work. The opposite also works. One member can own several partitions, as the analytics group shows: a single member reading all three. Groups remain completely independent of one another. Analytics has its own assignment and its own committed offsets. Adding members to fulfilment, or removing them, changes nothing for analytics. The practical consequence links back to chapter two. The partition count sets the maximum parallelism of every group that will ever read the topic. That is one reason to choose it with room to grow, rather than discovering the limit when a consumer group needs to scale.

Assignments are not permanent. When a member joins, leaves, or is judged to have failed, the group rebalances, and partitions move. The risky moment is handing over a partition that still has work in flight. Walk through this one. Member three starts and joins the group fulfilment. The group decides partition two should move from member two to member three. Member two is processing offset forty-one. Before it gives the partition up, the consumer calls its rebalance listener, on partitions revoked. That is the place to finish or abandon the work in progress, and to commit, here forty-two. Only then does member three receive partition two, and it starts reading at the committed offset, exactly where member two stopped. Skip that step, and two things can go wrong. Member three starts from an older commit and repeats work. And if member two had handed records to worker threads, those workers may still be busy when member three starts, so the same orders are processed twice at once. One more detail: the classic protocol's default assignor, range, makes every member give up every partition during each rebalance, not just the one that moves.

Kafka four has two protocols for running a consumer group, and you choose between them with the group protocol setting. They behave the same from the poll loop's point of view: poll, commit and offsets all work identically. What differs is who coordinates the group. In the classic protocol, which is still the client's default in Kafka four point one, one member of the group is elected leader and computes the assignment for everyone, using the client's partition assignment strategy. The session timeout and heartbeat interval are client settings. And a rebalance involves the whole group, whether cooperatively or not. In the newer consumer protocol, the broker computes the assignment, using one of its own assignors, uniform or range, chosen with group remote assignor. Session timeout and heartbeat interval move to the broker too. Rebalances become incremental, so only the members affected by a change do anything. The practical trap when switching is this: settings that only make sense for classic, such as session timeout or assignment strategy, are rejected at start-up, so a configuration that worked yesterday fails to start.

The group checks each member in two separate ways, and it is worth keeping them apart, because a slow handler fails only one of them. Heartbeats are sent by a background thread. They prove that the process is alive and connected. If none arrive for the session timeout, forty-five seconds by default, the member is removed. Calls to poll come from your loop. They prove the application is actually making progress. If the loop does not call poll within max poll interval, five minutes by default, the member leaves the group, even though its heartbeats are fine. Now take a slow handler. Poll returns five hundred records, and each one takes a second, perhaps because of a slow external service. That is over eight minutes before the next poll. At five minutes, the member leaves. Its partition is reassigned, and another member starts again from the last committed offset, repeating the batch. When the original handler finally finishes, its commit is rejected, because it no longer owns the partition. The batch has been processed twice, and if it keeps happening, the group can rebalance endlessly.

The fix for slow work is never to make the time limit longer and hope. It is to keep polling on time, either by doing less per poll, or by doing the work in parallel, without breaking ordering or commits. Start with the simplest lever. Lowering max poll records means each batch is smaller, so it finishes comfortably inside the five-minute limit. When the work itself has to happen elsewhere, the consumer can pause a partition. A paused partition is skipped by poll, but poll keeps being called, so the member stays in the group. Once the backlog clears, resume it, and fetching starts again. If you do process in parallel, three rules keep it safe. Use a bounded pool of workers, so a burst of records cannot exhaust memory or open thousands of database connections. Route records to workers by key, so all of one order's events go to the same worker and stay in order. And commit carefully: only up to the highest offset whose earlier records are all complete. Committing past a record that is still in progress brings back exactly the data loss window from earlier.

When a member is assigned a partition, it has to decide where to start reading. If the group has a committed offset, that always wins. The auto offset reset setting only matters when there is no usable commit, and there are three ways that happens. A brand new group has never committed anything. A group that has been empty, with no running members, for longer than the offset retention period, seven days by default, has its committed offsets deleted. And a committed offset can point at records that retention has already deleted, if the group fell too far behind. In each case, auto offset reset decides. Latest, the default, starts with records that arrive from now on, skipping everything already in the partition. That is right for a dashboard, and quietly wrong for fulfilment, which would never ship the backlog. Earliest starts from the oldest record still retained, so it can reprocess a great deal. None makes the consumer fail, so that a person decides. For a critical consumer, failing loudly is often better than silently skipping or silently replaying a week of orders.

Sometimes you want a group to read records again, for example after fixing a bug that mishandled the last hour of orders. That means moving the group's committed offsets, and done carelessly it either replays far more than intended, or skips data entirely. Here is the safe sequence. First, stop every member of the group. The tool requires that, because a running member would immediately overwrite the reset with its own commits. Then run kafka consumer groups with reset offsets, but without execute. Without execute, the tool only prints the plan. Here, to datetime nine o'clock picks, for each partition, the first offset at or after that time: twelve, thirty-one and nine. Check those numbers against what you meant to replay, partition by partition. Then run exactly the same command again, adding execute, and restart the group. It will reprocess everything from those offsets onwards. Two cautions. A reset by time uses record timestamps, which come from producers. And every reader of the replayed records must tolerate seeing them twice, which, once again, is chapter six's subject.

Underneath the abstractions, a partition is something very concrete: a directory on a broker's disk. Its log is not one ever-growing file. It is split into segments, each named after the first offset it contains. Every segment has three files. The log file holds the records themselves, in offset order, exactly as the producer's batches arrived. The index maps offsets to byte positions in that file, so a consumer asking for offset five thousand two hundred can be served without scanning from the start. The time index maps timestamps to offsets, which is what makes resetting a group to a point in time possible. Only the newest segment, the active one, is ever written to. When it reaches one gibibyte, or after seven days, it is closed and a new active segment starts. This design is why Kafka is fast on ordinary disks. Writes are appends at the end of a single file, which is the access pattern disks handle best. Recent data is usually still in the operating system's page cache, so most reads never touch the disk. And closed segments are never modified. They are only read, and eventually deleted as a whole.

Durability in Kafka comes from copying each partition to several brokers. The replication factor says how many copies there are, three in this example, and each copy lives on a different broker. Ideally those brokers are in different racks or availability zones, so that one power or network failure cannot take out every copy. One copy is the leader. Producers write to it, and consumers normally read from it. The others are followers. A follower stays up to date by fetching from the leader, in much the same way a consumer does, and appending what it receives to its own log. Now the most important idea in this chapter: the in-sync replica set, or ISR. It is the leader plus every follower that is keeping up. A follower that has not caught up with the leader for thirty seconds is removed from the set. Here, broker one has fallen behind at offset four, so the ISR is just brokers two and three. When broker one catches up, it rejoins. The controller records the ISR for every partition, because it answers the question every election needs answered: which copies are complete?

No single setting makes Kafka durable. Three settings work together, and they are owned by different people. The replication factor belongs to the topic. Min in-sync replicas is set on the topic, or for the whole cluster. And acks is chosen by each producer. The common durable combination is replication factor three, min in-sync replicas two, and acks all. Read the matrix row by row. With all three replicas in sync, writes are accepted, and every acknowledged record is on three brokers. Lose one broker, and writes are still accepted, now with two copies. That is the point of the combination: one broker can fail without losing data and without stopping writes. Lose a second, and only the leader is in sync. Now the leader refuses writes with a not enough replicas error, because it cannot guarantee two copies. Reads carry on. Nothing acknowledged has been lost. It is a deliberate choice to stop rather than to accept writes that are one failure away from loss. Notice the ownership problem too. A single producer configured with acks one quietly opts out of all of this.

It is tempting to think acks all alone makes writes durable. Look at what it actually means: wait for every replica in the ISR. And the ISR is not fixed. With the default min in-sync replicas of one, it is allowed to shrink all the way down to the leader alone. Walk through it. In step one, all three replicas are in sync and writes are copied everywhere. In step two, both followers fall behind, perhaps because of a slow disk or a network problem, and after thirty seconds they are removed from the ISR. Now acks all means wait for one replica, the leader itself. In step three, the producer sends order ten forty-one paid, and it is acknowledged with a single copy. In step four, the leader's disk fails. An acknowledged payment has disappeared, and the producer was told it succeeded. Now replay it with min in-sync replicas set to two. Step three is refused, with not enough replicas. The producer retries until a follower catches up. Writes pause for a while, but acknowledged data is never held on fewer than two brokers. And because producers cannot set this, it belongs on the cluster or the topic.

The leader of a partition can hold records that are not yet safe, because its followers have not copied them. Kafka needs a way to keep consumers away from those records, and that is the high watermark. Each replica in the ISR has a log end offset, the offset it will write next. The leader and broker three are both at twelve. Broker one, still in sync but a little behind, is at ten. The high watermark is the lowest log end offset across the in-sync replicas: ten. Everything below it, offsets zero to nine, is on every in-sync replica, so it would survive the loss of any of them. Consumers can read it. Offsets ten and eleven are on the leader, and on broker three, but not yet on broker one. They are hidden from consumers until broker one catches up and the high watermark moves. This has two consequences worth remembering. A slow follower that is still in the ISR delays what every consumer can see. And in return, a consumer never reads a record that a leader failover could later take back. That is what makes what a consumer reads consistent across failures.

When the broker leading a partition fails, the partition has no leader, and nothing can be written to it or read from it until the controller elects a new one. The controller does not pick at random. In Kafka four point one it works through a fixed order of preference, safest first. First choice, any member of the ISR, because an in-sync replica has every record that was acknowledged. Second, a member of the ELR, the eligible leader replicas. These are replicas that dropped out of the ISR at a moment when the controller could prove they still had every acknowledged record, so they are safe to elect too. ELR is enabled by default on new clusters in four point one. Third, the last known leader, if it comes back. Usually the first choice works and failover takes seconds. But if none of these replicas is available, the default is to wait. The partition stays offline, refusing reads and writes, until a safe replica returns. The alternative, an unclean election, would bring the partition back with whatever an out-of-sync replica happens to have, which is the subject of the next section.

Sometimes the only replica left is one that was out of sync. Here, broker one survives, but it stopped at offset nine, while the leader had already acknowledged offsets up to eleven. There are two options, and the setting unclean leader election enable chooses between them. With it off, the default, the partition stays offline until the old leader, or another safe replica, comes back. That might take minutes, or hours if hardware has to be replaced. But nothing acknowledged is lost. With it on, broker one becomes leader immediately, and the partition is available again. The cost is that offsets ten and eleven, both acknowledged to the producer, are gone for good. It is worse than it sounds, because of what happens next. New writes are given offsets ten and eleven again, for different records. Consumers that had already read the old ten and eleven now hold data the log no longer contains, and their committed offsets point at records that changed. If the old leader eventually returns, it truncates its log to match the new leader. So enable it only where availability genuinely matters more than the data, such as some metrics streams.

Everything so far has been about the data plane: brokers storing partitions and serving clients. But someone has to decide which topics exist, where each partition's replicas live, who leads each one, and which replicas are in sync. That is the metadata plane, and in KRaft mode it is run by controllers. A production cluster usually has three or five of them. One is the active controller, which makes every decision, and the others are hot standbys, ready to take over. Every change, a topic created, a leader elected, an ISR shrunk, is appended to a metadata log. That log is replicated across the controllers using a consensus protocol, the same idea as partition replication, and a change is final once a majority of controllers has it. Brokers follow that log. Each broker fetches new metadata records and applies them, which is how it learns that it now leads a partition. Brokers also send heartbeats to the controller, so a broker that disappears can be fenced, and its partitions given new leaders. KRaft replaced ZooKeeper, which used to hold this metadata, and Kafka four no longer supports ZooKeeper at all.

The controller quorum works by majority. A change is only final once more than half of the controllers have it, so the quorum can only make decisions while a majority is alive. With three controllers, a majority is two, so the cluster tolerates one controller failure. With five, it tolerates two. Losing a majority does not immediately stop all traffic, but it freezes the cluster. No metadata change of any kind is possible. No topic can be created, no configuration changed. More seriously, no leader can be elected. Existing leaders may keep serving producers and consumers for the moment, but the first broker failure leaves every partition it led offline, because nothing can choose replacements. So the design follows directly. Place controllers on separate hosts, ideally in separate racks or zones, so one failure cannot take out a majority. Use an odd number, because four controllers need three for a majority, and so tolerate only one failure, the same as three. And protect controller storage carefully. The metadata log is the definitive record of the cluster's structure.

Retention is how a topic forgets, and it works on whole segments, never on individual records. The defaults keep seven days by time, with no limit on size. Here is how the broker decides. It looks at each closed segment, and deletes it once the newest record in it is older than the retention period. It is the eighteenth of October. The first segment's newest record is from the eighth, ten days ago, so the whole segment is deleted. The second segment's newest record is six days old, so it stays, including records that are now ten days old themselves. The active segment is never deleted at all, however old its records are. So data lives somewhat longer than the retention setting, never shorter. The earliest offset still kept defines the replay horizon: how far back any group, or any replay, can go. Retention bytes adds a size limit per partition, if you set one, which is useful when disk, rather than time, is the constraint. And the risk from chapter one returns here. A consumer group that falls behind the horizon does not just lag. The records it had not read are gone.

Retention by time suits event streams. Some topics are better thought of as current state, such as the latest status of every order, and for those Kafka offers log compaction. Set the cleanup policy to compact, and instead of deleting by age, the broker keeps the latest record for each key. Here is the order status topic before and after the log cleaner has run. Order ten forty-one had placed, then paid, so the placed record at offset one is removed and paid survives at offset three. Order ten forty-three only has one record, so it stays. Notice that surviving records keep their original offsets. Nothing is renumbered, so gaps in offsets are completely normal in a compacted topic. Deleting a key needs a special record, a tombstone: the key with a null value. Order ten forty had placed, then shipped, then a tombstone. After cleaning, only the tombstone remains, and it is kept for a while, so that slow readers still see the delete, before it is removed as well. A topic can also combine compact and delete, which keeps the latest value per key, but only for a limited age.

It would be easy to assume a compacted topic only ever holds one value per key. It does not, because compaction is a background job that only runs under certain conditions. The cleaner never touches the active segment, so recent records always include every update until that segment closes, by default after seven days or one gibibyte. It also waits until enough of a partition is dirty, meaning written since the last clean, half of it by default, because cleaning is expensive. Min compaction lag can hold records back for longer still, and tombstones are kept for delete retention milliseconds, one day by default, so that a reader that was briefly behind still sees the delete. So readers of a compacted topic must expect several values for the same key, and handle them by keeping the latest. They must expect null values, and treat them as deletions rather than crashing. And one point matters for governance in chapter nine. Compaction is not erasure. An old value, including personal data, can remain on disk for days after a newer value was written, and in any copies already made downstream.

Delivery guarantees sound like settings you switch on. They are not. They describe the order in which a consumer does two things, committing its offset and doing its work, judged by what a crash between those two steps costs. Commit first, then process, and a crash in between means the restarted consumer starts after the record. The order is never shipped. That is at most once: nothing is repeated, but things can be lost. Process first, then commit, and a crash in between means the restarted consumer reads the record again. The order is shipped twice. That is at least once: nothing is lost, but things can be repeated. Every consumer has one of these two orders, whether anyone chose it deliberately or not. For order processing, losing an order is rarely acceptable, so almost every system chooses at least once. The real engineering work is then making a repeat harmless. And whenever someone claims exactly once, the useful question is: once for what, and where? Exactly once always has a scope. This chapter builds that scope one piece at a time, starting inside Kafka and then moving outward.

Kafka transactions solve the consume, process and produce pattern: read orders, compute something, and write results to another topic. A transactional producer is configured with a transactional id, and it calls init transactions once, at start-up. Then each batch runs inside a transaction. Begin transaction. Send every output record, here priced orders. Then, and this is the key step, send offsets to transaction, which adds the consumer group's input offsets to the same transaction. Finally, commit transaction. Either all of it becomes visible together, the output records and the input offsets, or none of it does. If anything fails, abort transaction discards the outputs and the offsets together, and the loop rewinds to the last committed position and tries again. A crash halfway through a transaction leaves nothing half done to clean up, because the coordinator will abort it. A transaction that stays open too long is aborted too, after the transaction timeout, sixty seconds by default. Keep the scope in mind, though. A transaction covers Kafka topics and Kafka offsets. It never reaches a database write or a call to another service.

Transactions need one more piece to be safe: protection from zombies. A zombie is an instance everyone believes is dead, but which comes back and carries on working. It is a real risk. A long garbage collection pause, or a network partition, can make a healthy instance look dead for long enough that its work is given to a replacement. Here is how Kafka handles it. Instance A is in the middle of a transaction, using transactional id order pricer zero, at epoch four. It pauses. Instance B starts as its replacement, with the same transactional id, and calls init transactions. The coordinator aborts whatever A had in progress, and moves the id to epoch five. B processes the batch and commits, with epoch five, and it is accepted. Then A wakes up, unaware of any of this, and tries to commit with epoch four. The coordinator rejects it. A is fenced. It receives a producer fenced exception, and the only correct response is to close and stop. All of this depends on the transactional id being stable, the same id for the same piece of work, rather than a fresh random id on every start.

Transactional records are written into the log as they are sent, before anyone knows whether the transaction will commit. So a consumer has to decide whether to see them early, and that is the isolation level. Read uncommitted, which is the default, returns everything in the log, including records from transactions that were later aborted. For readers of transactional output, that defeats the purpose, so they must set read committed. Read committed only returns records from committed transactions, and silently skips aborted ones. Look at partition one of priced orders. A read committed consumer receives offset twenty, from a committed transaction. It skips twenty-one, which was aborted. Then it reaches twenty-two, from a transaction that is still open, and it stops. It cannot know yet whether twenty-two will commit, and to keep records in order it will not jump ahead to twenty-three, even though that transaction has committed. This position is the last stable offset. The consequence for design is that one slow or stuck transaction holds back every read committed reader of that partition, for up to the transaction timeout. Keep transactions short.

Exactly once is one of Kafka's most quoted features, and one of the most misread. Kafka's exactly once means something precise. When an application reads from Kafka topics, processes, and writes to Kafka topics, with its input offsets committed in the same transaction, each input record affects the output exactly once. A failure and retry produce no duplicate output, because the failed attempt was aborted as a whole. That holds under one assumption: that processing is deterministic, so a retried batch produces the same output as the first attempt would have. Now look outside the boundary. The pricer might also charge a card, send an email, or write a row to a database. None of those are part of the Kafka transaction. If the transaction aborts, the charge has still happened, and the email has still been sent. When the batch is retried, they happen again. So, to state it plainly, a Kafka transaction cannot atomically charge an external payment service. Everything outside Kafka needs its own protection against repeats, and the next two sections show the two standard techniques.

Here is the plan's central example: charging a card when an order paid event arrives. The payment service is outside Kafka, so a transaction cannot help, and both commit orders fail. Commit first, then charge, and a crash between the two means the restarted consumer skips the event. The customer is never charged, and the order ships for free. Charge first, then commit, and a crash between them means the restarted consumer charges again. The customer is charged twice. Swapping the order only chooses which failure you get. The fix is not in the ordering. It is in the call. Charge first, then commit, but send an idempotency key with the charge, and use the event id as that key. Payment providers that support idempotency keys remember them. When the same key arrives a second time, they return the result of the first charge instead of charging again. Now the repeat after a crash is harmless: charged once. Two conditions apply, and both are worth checking with the provider. It must actually support idempotency keys, and it must remember them for longer than your longest possible replay.

When the effect is in a database you control, you can do better than hoping. Make the deduplication record part of the same database transaction as the effect itself. The pattern is simple. Begin a database transaction. Insert the event id into a processed events table, where the event id is a unique key. If that insert fails with a duplicate key, the event has already been handled, so roll back and skip it. Otherwise apply the effect, here reserving stock, and commit both together. Only after that commit, commit the Kafka offset. Now walk through crashes. A crash before the database commit leaves nothing behind, so the replay simply does the work. A crash after the database commit, but before the offset commit, means the event is read again, the insert hits the duplicate key, and it is skipped. Either way, the stock is reserved exactly once. The one thing to plan is how long to keep event ids. If they are deleted before a replay could reach the event again, an old event looks new. Keep them at least as long as the topic's retention, the replay horizon.

Now the producing side. When a customer places an order, checkout has to do two things: save the order in its database, and publish order placed to Kafka. They look like two lines of code. They are two separate writes, to two different systems, and there is no transaction that spans both. Try both orders. Write the database first, then publish. If checkout crashes between the two, the order is saved, but no event was ever published. Fulfilment never hears about it, and the order never ships. Publish first, then write the database. A crash between the two means fulfilment ships an order that the orders database has no record of. Retrying does not close the gap, because the crash can always land before the retry happens. This is the dual write problem, and it is easy to miss, because it works in every test. Nothing goes wrong until a crash lands in exactly the wrong millisecond in production. Then the two systems quietly disagree, with no error anywhere, until a customer complains. The fix is to stop writing to two places at once.

The transactional outbox removes the dual write by turning two writes into one. Checkout writes the order row and the event into the same database, in a single database transaction. The event goes into an outbox table: its type, its key, its payload, and its event id. Either both rows commit, or neither does, so there can never be an order without its event, or an event without its order. Publishing to Kafka then becomes a separate step, done by a relay. The relay reads outbox rows that have been committed, in order, and publishes each one to the orders topic. Often the relay is change data capture, which reads the database's own change log rather than querying the table, and chapter seven looks at how that works. If the relay crashes after publishing a row but before recording its progress, it publishes that row again on restart. So publishing is at least once, and readers deduplicate by event id, which the outbox row carries unchanged. The price is a short delay. The event reaches Kafka after the database commit, typically within seconds, rather than at the same instant.

Some records fail every time, however often they are retried: a malformed payload, a reference to a product that does not exist, a bug in the handler. These are poison records, and they are dangerous, because a consumer processes a partition in order. If it retries a poison record in place, it never gets past it, and every record behind it in the partition waits, possibly for days. The common fix is to move the record aside. On failure, the consumer publishes it to a retry topic, which is processed again after a delay, say a minute, in case the failure was temporary. After a few attempts, it goes to a dead letter topic, where it waits for a person to inspect it. The main partition keeps flowing the whole time. Notice the price. Order ten forty-one's paid event failed and went to the retry topic, and while it waited, the shipped event for the same order was processed from the main topic. The paid event is processed a minute later, out of order. So whatever consumes the results must cope with that. And never retry invalid data: quarantine it straight away, with the error attached.

Kafka's retained log makes replay possible, and earlier chapters showed how to reset a group. But replaying a week of orders only reproduces the original results if the processing is deterministic, meaning the same event always produces the same outcome. Anything the code reads from outside the event can quietly change the answer. The current time is the usual culprit. A discount that depends on the clock gives a different price on replay, so use the event's own occurred at time instead. Reference data is the next. Replaying last week's orders against today's price list produces today's prices. Look up reference data as of the event time, which means keeping its history. Randomness, such as generated coupon codes, should be derived from the event id, so a replay generates the same code. Before running any replay, check three things. That it is bounded, by offsets or by time, and previewed. That every reader of its output deduplicates by event id. And that side effects such as emails and payment calls are switched off for the replay, or customers will receive every one of them again.

Kafka Connect is Kafka's framework for moving data between Kafka and other systems, without writing producer or consumer code yourself. Instead of programming the integration, you configure a connector. There are four pieces to know. A worker is a Java process that runs connectors. A source connector reads from an external system, here the orders database, and writes records into Kafka. A sink connector does the opposite: it reads from Kafka and writes into an external system, here a search index. And each connector splits its work into tasks, which do the actual copying. The orders search sink has two tasks, sharing the three partitions of the orders topic between them, much like members of a consumer group. The division of labour is the point of Connect. The framework handles the general problems: tracking offsets, retrying, scaling out across tasks, and restarting after failures. The connector plugin handles what is specific to the external system, its API, its protocol, and its quirks. One thing to be clear about from the start: most connector plugins are third-party software. Apache Kafka itself ships only a few, mostly as examples.

Connect can run in two modes, and the choice is mostly about where state lives and what survives a failure. In standalone mode there is a single worker, configured from properties files on its local disk, and it keeps source offsets in a local file. It is simple, which makes it good for development and for a few special cases, such as an agent on one particular machine. But if the process dies, every connector it was running stops until someone restarts it. In distributed mode, several workers join a group, coordinated through Kafka in much the same way as a consumer group. Connectors are created and managed through a REST API, which any worker will accept. Connector configurations, source offsets and task status are all stored in Kafka topics, so no single worker holds anything that cannot be recovered. And when a worker dies, the group rebalances, and its tasks are started again on the remaining workers. Here, worker three fails, and its task moves to worker one. That is why distributed mode is the normal choice for production, even when a single worker would have enough capacity.

A connector is created by sending its configuration, as JSON, to the Connect REST API. This one is a sink that loads the orders topic into a warehouse database, and it uses a third-party JDBC connector, so the class name here is illustrative. It helps to see the settings as three layers. Framework settings belong to Connect itself: the connector's name, tasks max, which caps how many tasks it may run, and the topics to read. Converters decide how the bytes in Kafka become structured records the connector can work with, and back again. Here the key is a plain string, and the value is plain JSON, without an embedded schema. Everything else belongs to the plugin, such as the connection URL and the insert mode, and only that plugin's documentation can tell you what they mean. Two practical warnings. The plugin must be installed on every worker in the cluster, because a task can be scheduled onto any of them. And the converter must match how the topic was actually written. A converter expecting a different format fails every single record, which is one of the most common Connect problems in practice.

A connector's progress lives in one of two quite different places, depending on its direction, and it is worth knowing which before you ever need to reset one. A source connector reads from an external system, so its offsets describe a position in that system, not in Kafka. For a database change data capture connector, that is a position in the database's log. For a file connector, it is a byte position in the file. Each connector defines its own format, and in distributed mode they are all stored in a compacted Kafka topic called connect offsets. A sink connector reads from Kafka, and under the hood it is an ordinary consumer group, named connect, dash, followed by the connector's name. So its offsets are normal Kafka offsets, and the consumer group tools from chapter four show its lag. Two more internal topics complete the picture. Connect configs holds every connector configuration. It must have exactly one partition, so that configuration changes are read in order, and it should be compacted. Connect status holds the state of every connector and task. Create all three deliberately, with the right settings, rather than leaving them to auto-creation.

The status endpoint is where operating a connector starts. It reports the state of the connector, and separately the state of every one of its tasks, and those can disagree. Here the connector is running, and so are tasks zero and two. But task one has failed, on worker two, and the trace field says why: the warehouse refused the connection. The partitions assigned to task one are not being processed at all, while everything still looks healthy at the connector level. That is why monitoring should watch task states, not just connector states. Then the lifecycle calls. Restart, with include tasks and only failed both set to true, restarts just the failed task, without disturbing the healthy ones. Pause and resume stop processing temporarily, but keep the tasks' resources allocated, so they resume quickly. Stop shuts the tasks down and releases their resources, and a connector must be stopped before its offsets can be edited through the API. The most important habit, though, is simple: find and fix the cause before restarting. A task restarted into the same error just fails again, and repeated restarts hide the problem.

Sometimes a record needs a small change on its way through a connector, and single message transforms handle that without any custom code. A transform takes one record and returns one record, changed, or none at all. Several can be chained, and they run in the order they are listed. This source connector chains three, all of which ship with Kafka. Mask field blanks out the email and phone fields of the value, so that personal details never reach Kafka at all. Insert field adds a field naming the origin database, which is useful once several regions feed the same topic. And filter drops records. On its own it would drop everything, so it is paired with a predicate, record is tombstone, which limits it to records with a null value. So only deletions are dropped. The important limit is in the name: single message. A transform sees one record at a time, with no access to other records, other topics, or external lookups. So joins, enrichment and aggregation do not belong here. Business logic belongs in a stream processor, or in an application, where it can be tested properly.
