By default, Connect fails fast. One record that cannot be converted, or that breaks a transform, stops the task, and nothing behind it in that partition is processed until someone intervenes. For many pipelines that is the safest default, because it makes problems impossible to miss. The error settings let a connector keep going instead. Errors tolerance set to all makes the task skip records that fail conversion or a transform, rather than failing. Errors retry timeout retries failing operations for a while before giving up, which helps with brief outages. And errors log enable writes each failure to the worker log, with its topic, partition and offset, so it can be found later. Sink connectors can also send failed records to a dead letter topic, together with headers describing the error. Now the limits. The dead letter topic is only available for sink connectors. Tolerance set to all, with no dead letter topic and no logging, silently throws records away, which is data loss with no record of it. And a dead letter topic is only useful if someone actually monitors it and handles what lands there.

Change data capture is the integration pattern that the outbox in chapter six relied on. Instead of querying a table, a CDC connector reads the database's own change log, the same log the database uses for replication, and turns each change into a Kafka record. The usual connectors, such as Debezium, are third-party, so the details here vary by connector and by database. A CDC connector starts with a snapshot. It reads every existing row and publishes each one as a read event. Then it switches to streaming, and publishes every insert, update and delete as it happens. Updates can carry both the row before and after the change. A delete becomes a delete event, followed by a tombstone, so that a compacted topic eventually forgets the row. Several properties depend on the source, and are worth checking in the connector's documentation. The handover from snapshot to log has to leave no gap and no unexplained duplicate. The database has to keep its log long enough for the connector to read it, even after an outage. And ordering is per row key, not global, with database transactions possibly spread over several records.

It is tempting to assume that Connect provides one delivery guarantee for every connector. It does not. What a connector actually promises depends on the plugin's implementation, and on what the external system can do. Walk through a sink. Task one of the warehouse connector has committed offset thirty. It writes offsets thirty to thirty-nine into the warehouse, ten rows. Offsets are committed periodically, not after every write, and before the next commit, its worker dies. When the task restarts on another worker, it resumes from thirty, and writes the same ten records again. So most sink connectors are at least once. Whether that matters depends on how the sink writes. With plain inserts, the warehouse now has duplicate rows. With upserts by key, the repeat simply rewrites the same rows with the same values, and is harmless. That is why upsert modes exist in so many sink connectors. On the source side, Kafka supports exactly-once source connectors, in distributed mode only, but only for connectors that implement it. The rule is to read each connector's documented guarantee, and never assume one.

With all of that in mind, when is Connect actually the right choice? It is at its best when the job is moving data between Kafka and a system that already has a good, well-tested connector. Copying a database table into Kafka, or loading a topic into a warehouse, are its home ground. The connector handles the external system's quirks, and the framework handles offsets, retries and scaling. It is the wrong tool for business logic. Deciding whether an order qualifies for a discount, or reacting to a payment failure, belongs in a custom consumer or a stream processor, where the logic can be tested, versioned and reviewed like any other code. Not everything needs streaming either. A nightly bulk export can be simpler and cheaper as a batch job. And for moving data between two software-as-a-service products, a managed integration service may mean nobody on your team runs anything at all. Connect is also not free. It is a cluster of workers to run, upgrade and monitor, with connector plugins whose versions must match on every worker. Weigh that operational cost along with the convenience.

Kafka Streams is a Java library for processing data in Kafka topics, and the word library matters. There is no separate processing cluster to run. A Streams application is an ordinary Java program, deployed however you deploy your other services, and it uses Kafka itself for storage, coordination and recovery. The program describes a topology, a graph of operators. This one reads the orders topic, keeps only paid orders, regroups them by SKU, totals each SKU in five-minute windows, and writes the running totals to a topic called sales per SKU. Each operator compiles down to the ordinary things you already know: consumer reads, producer writes, and some local state. The single most important setting is the application id. It names the consumer group the application uses. It prefixes the name of every internal topic the application creates, such as repartition and changelog topics. And every running instance with the same application id shares the work, exactly like members of a consumer group. Change the application id, and to Kafka it is a brand new application, with no committed offsets and no state.

Kafka Streams divides an application's work into tasks. Each task handles one partition of the input, so the orders topic, with three partitions, gives this part of the topology three tasks, named zero underscore zero to zero underscore two. Tasks are the unit of parallelism, and they are what moves around. Each running instance of the application runs a number of stream threads, one by default, and the tasks are spread over every thread of every instance sharing the application id. Here, two instances each run two threads. That is four threads for three tasks, so one thread is idle, for exactly the same reason a consumer group member can be idle: there is nothing left to assign. A topology with a repartition step, like the sales totals, is split into two sub-topologies at that point, with a second set of tasks for the part after the repartition. Scaling out is just starting another instance with the same application id. The group rebalances, and some tasks move to the new instance. As with any consumer group, the partition count sets the ceiling on parallelism.

The same records in a topic can be read in two different ways, and Kafka Streams gives each its own type. A KStream treats every record as an independent event. Read the order status topic as a stream, and all four records matter: two orders were placed, one was paid, one was cancelled. A KTable treats every record as an update to the value for its key, so only the latest value per key matters. Read the same topic as a table, and it says order ten forty-one is paid, and order ten forty-three is cancelled. The earlier records have been superseded. In other words, a KTable is a topic read as a changelog, which is exactly what a compacted topic from chapter five is designed to hold. The two are closely related, and this is called stream-table duality. Aggregating a stream produces a table, such as a running total per SKU. And every change to a table can itself be emitted as a stream of updates. So the choice between them is about meaning. Use a stream for events you need to react to, and a table for current state you need to look up.

Some operators need nothing but the record in front of them. Filter keeps or drops a record, and map values changes its value. These are stateless, and they run right where the record already is, inside the task that read it, with no extra cost. Grouping by a different key is another matter. Orders arrive keyed by order id, so the orders for one SKU are scattered across every partition, and therefore every task. To total sales per SKU, all of one SKU's orders have to end up in the same task. So when the key changes before grouping, Kafka Streams inserts a repartition step. It writes every record to an internal repartition topic, keyed by SKU, and the next sub-topology reads that topic back. Now the partitioner from chapter two guarantees that each SKU lands in exactly one partition, and so in one task. This is handled for you, but it is not free. Every record makes an extra round trip through Kafka, with the storage and latency that implies. So prefer map values over map whenever the key does not actually change, because map alone marks the stream for repartitioning.

An aggregate has to remember something between records: the running total for each SKU and window. Kafka Streams keeps that in a state store. Each task has its own store, and by default it is RocksDB, an embedded key-value database on the instance's local disk. Because the store is local, reading and updating a total is fast, with no network call to a remote database. But local disk alone is fragile. If the machine is lost, the store goes with it. So every update to the store is also written to a changelog topic in Kafka, named after the application id. It is compacted, so it holds the latest value for each key, here each SKU and window: mug blue in the nine o'clock window went from twenty-four to thirty-six. The local store gives speed, and the changelog gives durability. Together, they give state that is fast to use, and that can be rebuilt on any other machine. This is the same idea as the KTable from two sections ago. A changelog topic is just a table, stored in Kafka. The next section shows the rebuild happening.

Here is what happens when an instance is lost. Its tasks are reassigned to the remaining instances, just as a consumer group reassigns partitions. Instance two is given task zero underscore one. But the task's state store lived on the lost machine's disk, so before it can process anything, instance two has to rebuild it. It reads the task's changelog topic from the beginning, and replays it into a new local store. Once the store is rebuilt, it resumes processing from the input's committed offset. How long that takes depends on how much state there is, from seconds for small stores to many minutes for large ones, and during that time the task produces nothing. Standby replicas address this. With num standby replicas set to one, another instance keeps a warm copy of each store, kept up to date from the changelog, so a takeover only needs a small catch-up. Two limits to keep in mind. With the default at least once guarantee, records processed after the last commit are processed again. And restoration rebuilds state, not effects. If the application sent emails, rebuilding a store does not make those emails safe to repeat.

Windowed aggregation groups records by event time, which brings back the late record from chapter two. Three terms explain what happens to it. Event time is the record's own timestamp, when the order was actually paid. Stream time is the largest event time a task has seen so far. It only moves forward, and it moves as records arrive, not with the wall clock. And grace is how far behind stream time a record is allowed to be and still count. This window covers nine o'clock up to five past, with one minute of grace, so it closes once stream time reaches six minutes past nine. Follow the arrivals. A record at one minute past is added to the window. Then a record at six minutes thirty seconds arrives. It belongs to the next window, but it also moves stream time past six minutes, so the nine o'clock window closes. Then a record from four minutes past arrives, from a phone that was offline. It belongs to the closed window, so it is dropped, and the total for that window will never include it. Grace is a trade-off between completeness and how long results stay open to change.

Kafka Streams joins records by key, and there are two kinds of join worth knowing well. A stream-table join enriches each event with current state. Here, each order looks up its customer in a customers table, to find their loyalty tier. There is no window. The order is joined with whatever value the table holds at the moment the order is processed. If the customer's tier changes a minute later, the old order is not revisited. A stream-stream join pairs events from two streams that relate to each other in time. Here, each order is paired with its payment, provided they happened within ten minutes of each other. Because either side could arrive first, both sides are buffered for the window, so a stream-stream join always needs a join window. Both joins share one hard requirement: co-partitioning. The two inputs must use the same key, have the same number of partitions, and use the same partitioner, so that matching records land in the same partition number, and so in the same task. If they do not, matching records sit in different tasks, and simply never meet. Streams checks partition counts, but keys are your responsibility.

It is worth tracing exactly what a windowed join produces, because the cases that produce nothing are the ones that cause surprises. The inputs are orders and payments, both keyed by order id, joined with a ten-minute window and one minute of grace. Order ten forty-one was placed at fourteen minutes past nine, and paid two minutes later. The two records are inside the window, so the inner join emits one output record, combining the order and the payment. Order ten forty-three was paid seventeen minutes after it was placed, outside the window, so the join emits nothing at all for it. And order ten fifty has no payment, so again nothing. An inner join only ever shows matches, which means it cannot show the most interesting case for this business: orders that were never paid. If you want unmatched records in the output, choose a left join, which emits every order, with the payment side empty when there is no match, or an outer join, which does the same for both sides. For finding unpaid orders, the absence of a match is the signal, so a left join is the tool.

A common surprise with Kafka Streams is that a windowed total is not emitted once, as a final answer. It is emitted as a series of updates. Here, the nine o'clock window for the blue mug is emitted as twelve, then thirty-six, then forty-eight, as paid orders arrive. Each new value replaces the previous one for that window. How many updates actually appear depends on record caching and on the commit interval, so the exact sequence can vary from run to run, while the latest value is always right. The consequence for downstream readers is important. They must treat the output as a table, keeping the latest value per key and window. A reader that adds the updates together would report ninety-six instead of forty-eight. Then the processing guarantee. The default, at least once, means that after a crash some updates may be emitted again. Exactly once v2 uses Kafka transactions, from chapter six, so output and offsets commit together and nothing repeats. It commits far more often, every hundred milliseconds, and its readers must use read committed to benefit.

Stream processing code has a reputation for being hard to test. Kafka Streams makes it easier than you might expect, because a topology can be tested with no broker at all. Topology test driver runs the topology in memory. The test pipes input records in, each with a timestamp you choose, and reads the output topic back, and the whole test runs in milliseconds. That control over timestamps is what makes it valuable. Test window boundaries with records just inside and just outside the grace period. Test late and out-of-order records deliberately, because production will send them. Then gather restart evidence in a real environment: stop an instance mid-load, start it again, and check that the totals match a run with no failure. Finally, where does Kafka Streams fit? It is at its best for per-key processing services that live next to Kafka, read Kafka topics, and are deployed like any other service. Spark and Flink run as separate processing clusters, connect to many kinds of source and sink, and are often a better fit for large analytical jobs. Spark Structured Streaming is covered in its own course.

Securing Kafka starts with a simple question: who is on the other end of each connection? Every application, every Connect cluster, every Streams application, and the brokers themselves, each need their own identity, called a principal. Two separate questions are then asked. Authentication asks who this is, and it is answered once, when the connection opens, using a certificate or a SASL mechanism. Authorization asks whether this principal may do this particular thing, and it is checked on every single request: may it write to orders, may it read as the fulfilment group. Encryption, with TLS, protects both of those exchanges, and all the data, while it crosses the network. Now map the boundaries in this system. Applications connect to brokers. Brokers connect to each other to replicate. Brokers and controllers connect to the controller quorum. And Connect and Streams applications act on behalf of other applications, so they need identities of their own too. The reason to insist on one principal per service is containment. If one credential leaks, one service is exposed, and only that credential needs replacing.

A broker can accept connections on several ports at once, each called a listener, and each with its own name, port and security protocol. That lets different audiences connect in different ways. Here there are three. Internal is for applications inside the data centre, and for replication between brokers. External is for partners connecting from outside, through a different network path. And controller is used only by the controller quorum, and Kafka requires it to be separate from the inter-broker listener. The security protocol map says each listener's protocol, here SASL over TLS for both client listeners. The setting that causes most connection trouble is advertised listeners. A client bootstraps by connecting to any broker it can reach. But the metadata it receives back lists each broker by its advertised address, and from then on, the client connects to those addresses. So each advertised address must be reachable by that listener's audience. A partner outside must never be told an internal hostname. And because clients verify hostnames, the advertised name must also appear in the broker's TLS certificate.

Connection problems look mysterious, but most of them follow a small number of patterns, and the symptom usually points straight to the cause. The most common: the client bootstraps successfully, then every request times out. The first connection worked because the bootstrap address was reachable. The following connections go to the advertised addresses from the metadata, and those are not reachable from where the client is. If a handshake fails immediately, the usual cause is a mismatch of protocols, such as a client configured for plaintext connecting to a TLS listener. If the certificate is rejected, the certificate authority that issued it is missing from the client's truststore. And if hostname verification fails, the broker's certificate does not contain the name the client connected to, which is the advertised name. If only one broker misbehaves, compare its configuration with the others. Before changing anything, collect evidence. Check which addresses the metadata actually returns. Inspect the certificate chain with openssl s client. And test DNS and routing from the client's own host, not from your laptop, because the network path is often the difference.

SASL is the framework Kafka uses for clients to prove who they are, and Kafka supports several mechanisms. The right one depends mostly on where your organisation's identities already live. SCRAM uses usernames and passwords, but the broker stores only salted hashes, and in a KRaft cluster those are kept in the cluster's metadata log. It is self-contained, which suits self-managed clusters. OAUTHBEARER uses short-lived tokens issued by a central identity provider, which suits organisations with a single identity platform, and has the advantage that a leaked token expires on its own. GSSAPI is Kerberos, for organisations that already run it. PLAIN sends a username and password, and should only be used with an external check behind it, never with passwords written into broker files. Some handling rules apply whichever you pick. Always run SASL over TLS, using the SASL SSL security protocol, because otherwise credentials can be read off the network. Keep secrets in a secret store, never in code, container images or repositories. And design every credential so that it can be rotated without an outage, which is the subject of the last section.

Authorization in Kafka is done with access control lists, ACLs, and the permission matrix is the clearest way to design them. In KRaft clusters the authorizer is the standard authorizer, and its most important behaviour is the default: a resource with no ACLs at all is closed to everyone except super users. Nothing is open by accident. Now read the matrix row by row. Checkout writes to the orders topic, and has no other permissions at all. Fulfilment reads the orders topic, and it also needs read permission on its consumer group, because committing offsets is an operation on the group. Missing that is a very common mistake. The pricer reads orders and writes priced orders, and because it uses transactions, it also needs write permission on its transactional ids. Analytics reads orders as its own group. Read and write each imply describe, so describe rarely needs granting on its own. The habits that keep this manageable are to grant exactly what each service's code actually does, topic by topic and group by group, and to keep super users few and audited, because a super user bypasses every ACL.

ACLs are managed with the kafka ACLs tool, or the equivalent Admin API calls from automation. The connection settings for an administrative principal are omitted here, but in a secured cluster the tool authenticates like any other client. Two shorthands save a lot of typing. The producer flag grants write, describe and create on the named topic, which is what a producer normally needs. The consumer flag grants read and describe on the topic, and read on the named group. So the second command gives fulfilment everything it needs in one line, including the group permission that is so often forgotten. List shows what a resource currently allows, which is the first thing to run when a client reports an authorization error. A few habits make ACLs safe to operate. Use prefixed resource patterns for families of names, such as every topic starting with an application's prefix, rather than a bare wildcard. Keep ACL definitions in version control, and apply them from a pipeline, so every change is reviewed and can be traced. And review the listing regularly, because ACLs only accumulate. Nothing removes a stale permission except a deliberate change.

When a service reports that it cannot read a topic, the cause is in one of four layers, and each layer produces its own kind of error with its own fix. Reading the exact exception, and fixing only that layer, saves hours of changing the wrong thing. Start at the bottom. If the client cannot reach the broker at all, you see timeouts or refused connections, and the fix is in addresses, firewalls or DNS. If the network works but TLS does not, the handshake fails, and the fix is in certificates and truststores. If TLS works but the credential is wrong, you see a SASL authentication exception, and the fix is the credential or the mechanism. And if the client is authenticated but not permitted, you see an authorization exception. A topic authorization exception means its ACLs on the topic are missing. A group authorization exception, from a consumer that can read the topic perfectly well, means it lacks read on its group. The layers fail in order: each one can only fail once every layer beneath it is working. That is also why changing ACLs can never fix a TLS problem.

Frameworks make least privilege slightly harder, because they create topics and groups of their own. Kafka Streams creates repartition and changelog topics, and Connect creates its configuration, offsets and status topics, plus a consumer group for every sink connector. The good news is that their names follow known patterns. Every internal topic of a Streams application starts with its application id, and its consumer group is named after it. Connect's internal topics and groups share the connect prefix by default. So prefixed ACLs can grant exactly those names, and nothing beyond them. The sales totals principal gets create, read and write on topics starting with sales totals, and read on the group with that name. Compare that with the shortcuts people reach for under deadline pressure. Cluster-wide create lets the service create any topic at all. A wildcard topic ACL lets it read every topic in the cluster, including ones holding sensitive data. And a single principal shared by every connector means one leaked secret opens every integration at once. Separate principals per connector take more setup, and are worth it where the cluster allows.

On a cluster shared by many teams, isolation becomes a design problem of its own. Without limits and clear ownership, one team's mistake becomes everyone's outage. Quotas are the technical limit. A byte-rate quota caps how fast a principal may produce, and how fast it may fetch, here ten mebibytes per second in and twenty out for analytics, enforced per broker. A client that goes over its quota is throttled rather than failed: the broker delays its responses until it is back under the limit. So a runaway analytics job slows itself down instead of saturating the brokers for everyone else. A request quota caps the share of broker request-handling threads one client can use, which protects against clients that send huge numbers of small requests. Ownership is the organisational limit. Every topic has one owning team, recorded somewhere people can actually find it, as chapter two described. And changes to topics, ACLs and quotas are treated as code: written down, reviewed, and applied by a pipeline. The reviewer's main question is the effect on other teams, through keys, retention and schemas.

Personal data in an event stream is far easier to add than to remove. Suppose a customer asks for their data to be deleted, and their details are in the orders topic. Kafka has no command to delete one record from a log. Retention removes whole segments, but only once they age out, on its own schedule. Compaction with a tombstone removes older values for a key, eventually, but only on compacted topics, and only when the cleaner runs. Deleting the topic removes everything in it, and still leaves every copy that has already left it: mirrored clusters, sink databases, search indexes and backups. So the controls that actually work happen earlier. The best is to keep sensitive data out of events in the first place, referring to customers by id, as chapter two advised. Where a sensitive field must travel, encrypt it, with a key per customer, and to forget the customer, delete their key, which makes every copy of the field unreadable at once. Give sensitive topics short retention. And keep audit evidence, from the authorizer's logs, of which principals read which topics, because questions about access always come later.

Every credential will need rotating eventually, on a schedule, or urgently after a suspected leak, and the way to do it without an outage is always the same pattern: overlap, move, prove, remove. For a SASL principal, start by creating a new principal and credential alongside the old one, and store the credential in the vault. Give the new principal exactly the same ACLs, and compare the listings to prove they match. Then roll the service's instances onto the new credential, one at a time, checking each one connects. Now comes the step people skip. Watch the old principal, and only remove it once it has made no connections for a reasonable period, a day here, because a forgotten batch job or a second deployment may still be using it. Then remove the old ACLs and credential, and record the change. Certificates follow the same shape. Add the new certificate authority to every truststore first, so that both old and new certificates are trusted. Then roll new certificates onto brokers and clients, one broker at a time. Remove the old authority last, once nothing presents a certificate it signed.

Every capacity decision in this chapter starts from one thing: a workload model. It is simply the expected traffic, written down as numbers, together with where each number came from, so that anyone can check it and change it. A few dimensions matter most. Rates, both the average and the peak. The orders topic averages two hundred records a second, but on a sale day it peaks at two thousand, and a system sized for the average fails on exactly the day that matters most. Record size, because bytes, not record counts, fill disks and networks. Fan-out: three consumer groups read every record, so the brokers serve three times as many bytes as they receive. Key skew, how much traffic the busiest key carries, here the top product is five percent of all orders. And retention, which turns rates into disk. To make the model trustworthy, take rates from real order history, by hour, rather than from a guess. Measure record sizes on real, serialized records, including headers, rather than estimating them from the schema. And label every figure clearly as an assumption until it has been measured, like the ones on screen.

A storage estimate is a chain of multiplications, and the way to keep it honest is to write the unit at every step. Here is the chain for the orders topic. Two hundred records a second, at one kibibyte each, is two hundred kibibytes per second. Multiply by eighty-six thousand four hundred seconds, and that is sixteen and a half gibibytes a day. Seven days of retention makes one hundred and fifteen gibibytes. Compression, which was measured on real sample records rather than assumed, halves that, to fifty-eight. Replication factor three triples it, to one hundred and seventy-three gibibytes across the cluster, or about fifty-eight per broker, if partitions are evenly balanced. Then be explicit about what the estimate leaves out, because that is where real clusters run out of disk. Every other topic, including priced orders, repartition topics and changelogs. Active segments, which are kept beyond the retention period, as chapter five showed. Growth over the next year. And headroom. Never plan to fill a disk, because a full disk on a broker takes its partitions offline, and recovery needs space to work in.

Chapter two showed that adding partitions later moves keys, and chapter four showed that the partition count caps a group's parallelism. So it is worth sizing the count deliberately, from the slowest consumer, at peak. Peak traffic is two thousand records a second. Fulfilment is the slowest consumer, because each order involves a warehouse system, and one member was measured handling about one hundred records a second. So at peak, the group needs twenty members working at once, which means at least twenty partitions. Choosing twenty-four leaves room to grow without repartitioning, and divides evenly among a few broker counts. Why not choose five hundred and never think about it again? Because partitions are not free. Every partition has files, segments and indexes, on every one of its replicas. Producers and consumers hold buffers for each partition they use. When a broker fails, every partition it led needs a new leader, so failover has more work to do. And with traffic spread across more partitions, each partition's batches are smaller, which costs efficiency. A count based on measurement, with headroom, beats a big round number.

Chapter three covered the producer's side of the latency and throughput trade-off: linger and batch size decide how full each batch is, and compression trades CPU for bytes. The consumer has the mirror image of those settings. Fetch min bytes tells the broker not to answer a fetch until at least that much data is ready. The default is one byte, which means answer immediately. Fetch max wait caps how long the broker will wait for that amount, five hundred milliseconds by default. Raise the minimum, and fetches become fuller and cheaper, at the cost of a little delay when traffic is light. Max partition fetch bytes caps how much one fetch returns for each partition, one mebibyte by default. And max poll records caps how many records each poll hands to the loop. Here is the practical caution. For most applications, fetching is not the bottleneck. Processing is: the database write, the call to the warehouse system, the business logic. So before tuning any fetch setting, measure how long the handler takes per record. Tuning fetches for a consumer that is busy processing changes nothing at all.

When clients get slower, the cause is often a broker running short of something, and each resource has a metric that shows it, ideally before clients notice. Request handler threads do the actual work of each request, and network threads move bytes to and from sockets. For both, the broker reports an average idle percentage. Healthy brokers have plenty of idle time. As it falls toward zero, requests start queueing. Network capacity shows in bytes in and out per second, compared with the link speed, remembering that fan-out and replication multiply outbound traffic. Disk and memory go together. Kafka relies on the operating system's page cache, so most reads of recent data never touch the disk. When consumers fall behind and read old data, or memory is short, reads start hitting the disk, and everything slows. The most useful single view is request time, split into parts. Total time for a produce request is the sum of time queued waiting for a thread, local time writing on the leader, remote time waiting for followers under acks all, and time sending the response. Whichever part grew tells you where to look.

Three different measurements all get loosely called lag, and confusing them leads to bad alerts. They answer different questions. Consumer lag is a count: how many records the group is behind, the log end offset minus its committed offset. Here, twelve hundred records. Processing latency is how long the consumer takes to handle one record, here forty milliseconds. And freshness is how old the results are: the time between an event happening and its effect being visible, here six seconds. These can move independently. Lag only becomes a time once it is divided by the incoming rate. Twelve hundred records at two hundred a second is about six seconds, which agrees with the freshness here. But on a quiet topic, lag can be tiny while the one waiting record is an hour old, so results are stale. And a burst can make lag jump to thousands while freshness barely changes, because the burst clears in a few seconds. Customers notice freshness. They never see a record count. So freshness, measured from event time, is the measure to alert on, with lag as a supporting signal.

Lag growing is a symptom, not a cause, and the first job is to decide where to look. A simple technique works surprisingly often: plot consumer lag next to produce latency, over the same period. These two charts are supplied examples, not measurements from a real system, but they show the two patterns you will meet most. In incident A, lag starts climbing at minute ten and keeps climbing, while produce latency stays completely flat. Producers are being served normally, so the brokers are healthy. The consumer is the bottleneck. Perhaps its handler got slower, or it is failing and retrying, or garbage collection is stalling it. In incident B, lag climbs, and produce latency climbs with it. Now every client of the cluster is affected, which points at the brokers: request threads saturated, a slow disk, or a congested network. From there, each pattern turns into a hypothesis to test. For A, look at the application's handler time, its errors and its garbage collection. For B, look at the broker resource metrics from two sections ago. Either way, confirm the hypothesis before changing anything.

A total lag figure hides where the lag actually is. This group's total lag is just over forty-eight thousand records, which looks like the whole group is struggling. Describe the group, and the per partition breakdown tells a different story. Partitions zero and two are a handful of records behind, completely healthy. Partition one is forty-eight thousand records behind, and still growing. That is not a capacity problem across the group. It is skew, concentrated on one partition, and so on the one member that owns it. This is exactly where the most common fix fails. Adding members to the group cannot help, because partition one can only ever have one reader within the group, as chapter four explained. The new members would sit idle. What does help? In the short term, making the handler faster helps that partition specifically. To understand the cause, sample records from partition one and look at the keys. Very often one key, such as a single product in a flash sale, or a single enormous business customer, is carrying far more than its share. The lasting fix is the key design from chapter two.

Under-replicated partitions is one of the most important broker metrics. It counts partitions where at least one replica has fallen out of the in-sync set. Any value above zero deserves a look, but the number alone does not say why. The pattern across brokers does. If every partition with a replica on one particular broker is under-replicated, that broker is down or restarting, and the count should fall as it recovers. If the followers on one broker are lagging, but the broker is up, its disk or network is slow, and its follower fetch times will show it. If under-replication is spread across every broker, the cause is cluster-wide: heavy load, or a large partition reassignment copying data around. Two related metrics say when it has become urgent. Under min ISR partition count above zero means some partitions are below min in-sync replicas, so acks all writes to them are already being refused, as chapter five described. And offline partitions count above zero means partitions with no leader at all. Whatever the pattern, find the cause before restarting brokers, or a slow broker becomes a missing one.

Tuning advice is easy to find and easy to misapply. The only way to know whether a change helps your system is a controlled comparison: the same workload, measured the same way, with exactly one change between the two runs. Kafka ships a load generator for this, the producer performance test. Here it sends one million records of one kibibyte each, at a fixed two thousand records a second, which is the peak rate from the workload model. The two runs are identical except for linger milliseconds, five then twenty. The tool reports throughput and latency percentiles. Compare the percentiles, such as the ninety-ninth, not just the average, because an average can improve while the slowest requests get worse. A few rules keep the comparison fair. Use realistic record sizes, keys and rates, because a benchmark of tiny records says little about real ones. Run long enough to get past warm-up effects, including the page cache filling. And never let a tuning experiment win by weakening a guarantee. A configuration that is faster because it changed acks to one has not been tuned. It has been made less durable.

Capacity planning is usually framed as keeping up with traffic. Recovery is the part that gets forgotten: how quickly a consumer catches up after it has been down. Take fulfilment, down for one hour while orders keep arriving at two hundred a second. That leaves a backlog of seven hundred and twenty thousand records. When it comes back, new orders are still arriving, so it can only spend its spare capacity, its total capacity minus the incoming rate, on the backlog. With a capacity of a thousand records a second, eight hundred a second are spare, and the backlog clears in fifteen minutes. With four hundred, it takes an hour. With two hundred and fifty, only fifty a second are spare, and it takes four hours, during which orders are shipping late. And a group sized at exactly two hundred a second, just enough to keep up, never catches up at all. So size consumers with genuine spare capacity. Keep retention comfortably longer than any plausible catch-up, so the backlog cannot expire before it is read. And remember that an outage hurts most on a peak day, when spare capacity is smallest.

Operating Kafka day to day is mostly a matter of single commands: change a topic's retention, add partitions, reset a group, delete a topic. Each is easy to type. What separates a safe operation from an incident is knowing how hard each change is to undo. Raising retention is easy to undo, though check disk headroom first. Lowering it is not, because the broker deletes newly expired segments at its next retention check, within minutes, and a slow reader loses whatever it had not read yet. Adding partitions can never be undone, and it moves keys, as chapter two showed. Resetting a group's offsets can only be reversed if somebody saved the old offsets first. And deleting a topic is permanent. So put a safeguard in front of every irreversible change. Keep topic and configuration changes as code, in version control, reviewed before a pipeline applies them. Record the current state before changing anything: the configuration, the partition assignment, the group offsets. Use previews and dry runs wherever a tool offers them, as the offset reset did in chapter four. And make sure the topic's owner agrees, and its readers are told.

When the cluster needs more capacity, adding a broker is the obvious step, and it surprises people that the new broker starts out doing nothing at all. Kafka never moves existing partitions by itself. The new broker will only receive partitions created after it joined, unless existing ones are deliberately reassigned to it. The tool for that is kafka reassign partitions, and it works in three steps. Generate takes a list of topics and the brokers to spread them over, and proposes a plan. Execute starts carrying it out. For each partition that gains a replica on broker four, broker four copies every byte of that partition from the leader, so the throttle option caps how much bandwidth replication may use, here fifty megabytes a second, to protect clients. Verify reports progress, and once the reassignment has completed, it also removes the throttle. That last detail matters more than it seems. Forget to run verify, and the throttle stays in place, quietly limiting replication. The next time a broker fails and its replicas need to catch up, they catch up slowly, and the cluster stays under-replicated far longer than it should.

The plan that generate produces is a preview, and it is worth reading line by line before executing it. Here, each partition of the orders topic gains a replica on broker four, and gives one up elsewhere. Partition zero's preferred leader also moves to broker four, which means client traffic for that partition will shift to the new broker too. The tool also prints the current assignment, and that output deserves saving, because it is the only rollback plan you have. Rolling back is not an undo button. It is simply another reassignment, back to the old placement, so every byte that was copied to broker four is copied back again. It takes about as long as the original move, under the same throttle. If a reassignment is still in progress and causing trouble, cancel can stop it, which leaves partitions on whatever replicas they had reached. The safest habit follows from all of this. Move a few partitions at a time, rather than the whole cluster in one plan. Watch client latency and under-replicated partitions after each batch, and only continue once things are calm.

Kafka is designed to be upgraded without downtime, by rolling through the brokers one at a time, and the upgrade notes for four point one give the sequence. Start by reading the release notes for every version you are crossing, not just the target. Then upgrade the brokers one at a time: stop one, update its software, restart it, and wait until there are no under-replicated partitions before moving to the next. Waiting is what keeps every partition fully replicated while each broker is briefly away. Once every broker runs the new version, check that the cluster's behaviour and performance are as expected. Only then run the final step, kafka features upgrade, which moves the cluster's metadata version forward. That step is one-way: the notes are explicit that metadata downgrade is not supported after it. Two checks are specific to this baseline. Kafka four removed old protocol versions, so clients, including Streams and Connect, must be on two point one or newer. And the four point one point oh release notes warn of a serious memory leak in Kafka Streams, advising four point one point one instead. That is exactly why reading release notes comes first.

A runbook turns an incident into a sequence of steps, and the important part is that every step names the evidence that proves it worked. It is written and rehearsed before the incident, because nobody designs a good procedure at three in the morning. Here is one for a broker that stops responding, on a cluster with replication factor three and min in-sync replicas two. Detect: the alert fires because broker two is no longer registered. The first number to check is offline partitions, which should be zero, because every partition still has two other replicas. Assess: under-replicated partitions shows which partitions lost a copy. Protect: check that writes are still being accepted, meaning no partition has fallen below min in-sync replicas. If any have, producers are being refused, and that changes the urgency. Repair: restart the broker, or replace it and reassign its partitions. Confirm: the broker rejoins, its replicas catch up, and under-replicated partitions returns to zero. Controller failures have their own runbook. Losing one of three is calm work. Losing two means no metadata changes at all, and is urgent.

At the end of an incident there is a tempting moment when every dashboard turns green. The brokers are running, the consumer pods report ready, the error logs are quiet, and the in-sync replica sets are full again. All of that is process evidence. It shows that the components are alive. It does not show that customers are being served, and the two can disagree for hours. Recovery should be declared on service evidence instead. Are orders being produced and acknowledged, end to end? Is fulfilment's freshness, the measure from chapter ten, back within its target? Has the backlog that built up during the outage actually drained? And do the order counts reconcile, comparing the orders database with what reached Kafka and what fulfilment processed, so that nothing was silently lost? Only when those are true has the service recovered. Then write it down while it is fresh: a timeline of what happened, what was done, and the evidence for recovery. That record is what turns one incident into a better runbook for the next one.

For surviving the loss of a whole region, or a whole cluster, Kafka offers MirrorMaker two. It runs as a set of Kafka Connect connectors that read from one cluster and write to another. Here it copies the orders topic from the eu west cluster to the us east cluster. Three details shape every design built on it. First, records land in a renamed remote topic. With the default replication policy, orders from eu west becomes eu west dot orders in the target. That rename keeps the two regions' orders apart, so a consumer that wants both has to subscribe to both names. Second, consumer group offsets are copied too, but they cannot be copied directly, because the same record has different offsets in the two clusters. A checkpoint connector translates them periodically, so translated offsets are only as recent as the last checkpoint. Third, and most important, copying is asynchronous. The target is always behind the source, here by about twenty seconds. Nothing waits for the copy, so producers in eu west are never slowed down by it. That is the strength of mirroring, and, as the next section shows, its cost.

Now suppose the eu west cluster is lost at ten o'clock, and fulfilment fails over to us east. Because mirroring is asynchronous, the failover cannot be exact, and the timeline shows how it goes wrong in both directions. The last checkpoint translated fulfilment's offsets as of nine fifty-nine. Orders placed before then were already processed, and the translated offsets correctly skip them. Orders placed between nine fifty-nine and nine fifty-nine and forty seconds were mirrored, but fulfilment's translated offsets do not reflect that it processed them, so it reads them again. Without deduplication, they ship twice. And orders from the last twenty seconds never reached us east at all, because mirroring was twenty seconds behind. They are missing until eu west comes back. So failover is always followed by reconciliation. Deduplicate by event id, from chapter six, so the repeats are harmless. Find the gap by comparing the order database with what fulfilment processed. Replay the missing orders once eu west returns. And decide in advance who is allowed to declare a failover, and under what conditions, because doing it too early creates more reconciliation work.

Recovery objectives turn vague hopes into numbers that can be checked. The recovery point objective, or RPO, is how much data a scenario may lose. The recovery time objective, or RTO, is how long recovery may take. The useful exercise is to list scenarios, give each an objective, and compare it with what the design actually delivers. Losing one broker, or even a whole availability zone, costs no acknowledged data, because replication factor three across three zones, with min in-sync replicas two, keeps two copies of everything. Losing a whole region costs up to the mirroring lag, about twenty seconds of orders, and recovery takes as long as a manual failover and reconciliation. Bad data, such as a bug that wrote wrong prices for an hour, is recovered by fixing the bug and replaying, but only while the source records are within the seven-day retention. Then list the gaps honestly. Replication copies mistakes as faithfully as good data, so it is not a backup. Restoring Kafka is not enough if sink databases disagree with it. And an objective that has never been rehearsed is only a guess.

Running Kafka yourself is not the only option, and managed Kafka services are common. The useful way to compare them is by responsibility. A managed service takes over the brokers: the hardware, the operating systems, the broker processes, and their monitoring. It takes over upgrades and patching, usually on the provider's schedule rather than yours. And it takes over part of capacity, although you still choose a size and pay for it. What never moves to the provider is the data design, which is most of this course. Topics, keys, partition counts and schemas are still your decisions, with the same consequences for ordering and evolution. ACLs, and the protection of sensitive data, are still yours. And consumer correctness, meaning commits, duplicates, replays and idempotent effects, is entirely yours, because it lives in your applications. Weigh three more things. Cost, comparing service fees with the staff time self-management really takes. Portability, because features only one provider offers make leaving harder. And limits, because a managed service may restrict versions or configuration settings that this course has relied on.

This is the whole course in one picture: the orders platform, with every piece justified by a failure it prevents. On the writing side, checkout saves each order and its event in one database transaction, using the outbox from chapter six, so no order can exist without its event. A change data capture connector, from chapter seven, publishes outbox rows to Kafka, at least once. In Kafka, the orders topic is keyed by order id, from chapter two, so each order's events stay in sequence, with twenty-four partitions from the capacity plan in chapter ten. The cluster uses replication factor three and min in-sync replicas two, from chapter five, runs in KRaft mode, and gives every service its own principal and ACLs, from chapter nine. A dead letter topic keeps poison records from blocking their partitions. On the reading side, fulfilment, sales totals and notifications are each their own consumer group, so they progress independently, and each one treats a repeat as harmless, by deduplicating on event id or by making its effects idempotent. Sales totals are computed by a Kafka Streams application, with windows and grace, from chapter eight.

The last step is to review the design as a whole, and the rule for this review is simple: every answer must be evidence, not intention. For contracts, can the schema change safely? The evidence is a compatibility check that runs in the build, not a promise to be careful. For ordering, which events must stay in order? The evidence is the key and topic choice, written down with its reasoning. For duplicates, what happens when a record is processed twice? The evidence is a test that replays records and shows the outcome is unchanged. For durability, which failures lose data? The failure matrix, and the settings that produce it. For security, who can read orders? The ACL listing, and the audit log. For capacity, how quickly does fulfilment catch up after an hour's outage? A measured recovery run. And for recovery, has it been proven? A rehearsal, with a record of what happened. From here, continue by taking another workload through the same questions, revisiting its contracts and its failure assumptions, and always checking current documentation before implementing or upgrading a real system.
